en: The Dharma-discourse on the Description of the Benefits of Establishing Images of the Tathāgata & The Avadāna of the Divine Food (Divyabhojanāvadāna), according to Śāstrī, item 81, dated NS 385 = 1265 CE.
Tibetan: similar to D 320.
Péter-Dániel Szántó:

Judging from the introductory questions by Ānanda, this cannot be the comprehensive title of the sūtra; the missing contents are rather predictable (cf. also Tôh. no. 320, vol. SA, folios 197r.1–198v.4). See also Taishō no. 692, translated by Robert H. Sharf in *Buddhist Practice in Medieval Chinese Society*, edited by D. Lopez, pp. 261–267. Kieschnick, *Impact*, p. 78.
Homage be to the Buddha!

Thus have I heard: at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery. Then the venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One; having approached and bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, he stood to one side. Standing to one side, the venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One in this way.

“Blessed One, what is the root of merit for the offering of sweeping? What is the root of merit for the offering of a mandala? What is the root of merit for taking refuge and the precepts? What is the root of merit for the act of prostrating and joining the palms before the Tathāgata? Blessed One, what is the root of merit that is neither exhausted nor diminished within saṃsāra, and which leads to the inexhaustible nirvāṇa? What is the root of merit for making an image of the Tathāgata? The Blessed One said:

There are five benefits in the act of sweeping and offering. What are the five? Namely: one’s own mind becomes serene; the deities become joyful; one performs and accumulates karma that leads to a beautiful appearance; and after the dissolution of the body, one is reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world among the gods. Ānanda, whoever with a serene mind makes a square mandala dedicated to the Tathāgata—for him, Ānanda, I declare the continent of Uttarakuru as his domain of sovereignty. And after the dissolution of the body, he is reborn in the Heaven of the Thirty-three...

We shall not explain it ourselves. Rather, let us ask this very matter of the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, the All-Knowing, the All-Seeing, the Dispeller of all doubts, the Teacher; for in whatever way the Blessed One explains it to us, so shall we remember it. And we shall explain it in detail and analyze it for the faithful brahmins and householders.
"Venerable sir, we ask the Blessed One about this very matter: Venerable sir, how many benefits are to be known as resulting from a donor having an image of the Tathāgata made?
The Blessed One said:"

“Excellent, excellent, monks! You have set out for the benefit of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, and for the sake, benefit, and happiness of gods and humans, in that you consider this very matter worthy of being asked of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One. Therefore, monks, listen and attend well and properly; I shall speak.
Monks, there are five benefits for a person who causes an image of the Tathāgata to be made as a donor. What are the five?”

[§1] Monks, this is the first benefit for a person who gives a Tathāgata’s image: they become possessed of a great celestial mansion, of great renown, immeasurable, of great strength, of great energy, long-lived, illustrious, and abundant in happiness.

[§2] Furthermore, monks, he becomes wealthy, possessing great riches and great enjoyments; having abundant wealth and resources, abundant internal property, and an abundance of accumulated money, grain, gold, treasuries, and storehouses; having an abundance of elephants, horses, mules, female and male slaves, laborers, and servants; and having an abundance of friends, ministers, kinsmen, and blood relations. Monks, this is the second benefit for a person who has a likeness of the Tathāgata made.

[§3] Furthermore, monks, he becomes one who is desirable to behold, pleasing, of a fair complexion, with a golden hue, a head shaped like a parasol, long arms, and a broad forehead; his eyebrows and nose are well-proportioned, and he is endowed with all major and minor limbs and adorned with every ornament—this, monks, is the third benefit for the person who causes the image of the Tathāgata to be made by the donor.

Furthermore, monks, suppose there is a universal monarch (cakravartin) with a vast retinue, endowed with the seven jewels, surrounded by a thousand sons—whether they be his sons, wives, servants, or dependents—all of whom serve him and remain intent on obeying his commands. Monks, this is the fourth benefit for a person who gives for the purpose of creating an image of the Tathāgata.

[§5] Furthermore, monks, upon the dissolution of the body, he is reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world, among the gods. Having been reborn there, he becomes incomparable and preeminent among the other gods, sons of gods, and goddesses; as a king of gods, he shines forth by ten points: by divine lifespan, divine complexion, divine strength, divine happiness, divine sovereignty and dominion, and by divine forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles.
"O monks, this fifth benefit for the person who gives [the material] for the making of a likeness of the Tathāgata—consisting of forms, sounds, odors, and tangibles—is to be understood."
The Blessed One said this; with uplifted minds, those monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had spoken.

The Dharma discourse titled "The Description of the Benefits of the Tathāgata’s Reflection" is completed. In the year 384, on the tenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina, on Thursday.
